summary: Defines a way to attach the schema trees of a set of YANG modules at a chosen mount point inside another YANG module. This lets a device model contain complete sub-models, which is useful when a device hosts things like logical devices or network instances that each have their own structure. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Think of building with LEGO. You can snap a whole finished little model onto a spot on a bigger model instead of rebuilding its pieces there.

questions: how to mount a yang module inside another

why not use uses or augment in yang
subtitle: How to snap a whole set of YANG modules onto a single spot inside another module's data tree, without rewriting them.

tldr.problem: Some devices host several logical devices or network instances, each needing its own copy of modules such as ietf-interfaces. The YANG statements uses and augment can only do this by wrapping or duplicating the same hierarchy, which does not scale.
tldr.mechanism: A parent module marks a container or list as a mount point with the mount-point extension. Operational state data under /schema-mounts then says which schema is mounted there, either inline or as a shared schema.
tldr.outcome: Existing modules can be mounted unchanged, each mounted schema behaves like a top-level schema, and the server describes it with YANG library data. Only complete data models can be mounted.

facts.label: Mount point extension
facts.value: mount-point, only under container or list

today: RFC 8528 is a Standards Track document, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. RFC 8529 builds the network instance module on it.

sections.title: What Schema Mount Is
sections.content:
RFC 8528 defines schema mount, a way to add the schema trees of a set of YANG modules onto a mount point defined in another module's schema tree. It is an extensibility mechanism for YANG 1.1 (RFC 7950). Unlike existing mechanisms, it defines the link between the source and target modules outside those modules.

The idea is simple: label one data node in the parent schema as the mount point, then attach a complete data model to it, so that the labeled node effectively becomes the root of the mounted data model. The document is a Standards Track product of the IETF.
sections.eli5: Schema mount lets you pick one spot on a big model and stick a whole smaller model onto it, like clicking a finished LEGO house onto a baseplate.

sections.title: Why uses and augment Fall Short
sections.content:
YANG modules normally appear side by side, so the top-level nodes of each module are top-level nodes of the whole data model. YANG already has two ways to place a hierarchy elsewhere: uses pulls in a grouping, and augment adds contents to a target node. In both, the module with the statement defines the exact place where the nodes go.

The RFC's example is a device with several logical devices, each with its own copy of ietf-interfaces, all managed from the master device. Using uses, the whole module would need to be wrapped in a grouping. The RFC lists the drawbacks:

  • It does not scale, because every new module needs another uses statement in the logical device model.
  • Absolute references to nodes inside a grouping may break if the grouping is used in different locations.
  • Nodes in a grouping belong to the namespace of the module that uses it, which makes references from other modules hard or impossible.
  • Vendors would find it hard to add proprietary modules when the uses statements sit in a standard module.

With augment, the same hierarchy would have to be defined twice, which is not scalable either. Mounted modules, by contrast, need no special preparation, so ietf-interfaces can be mounted without modification.
sections.eli5: Copying every piece of a model onto each new spot is slow and breaks easily. Mounting is like putting the finished model on the shelf once and just pointing to it.

sections.title: Mount Points and Mounted Schemas
sections.content:
A mount point is a container or list that has the mount-point extension statement, defined in the ietf-yang-schema-mount module, in its definition. The extension may appear only under container and list. Its argument is a YANG identifier used as a label, and a module MAY contain several mount points with the same label. The statement does not create a new data node. A mount point can be made conditional with if-feature or when.

The mount-point extension MUST NOT be used in a YANG version 1 module, because RPC operations and notifications from mounted modules could not then be used. Modules written in any YANG version can still be mounted.

The RFC names three moments when a mounted schema could be specified: design time, implementation time and run time. This document supports only the latter two. Design-time mounts are out of scope. It also allows only complete data models to be mounted, not sub-hierarchies of a module, and leaves how and when mount points are instantiated out of scope.

If a mount point has no entry in the mount-point list, the mounted schema is void, and instances of that mount point MUST NOT contain any data except what the parent schema defines.
sections.eli5: A mount point is a labeled socket on the big model. The socket does not hold anything by itself; it just says where a smaller model can plug in.

sections.title: The schema-mounts Data Model
sections.content:
The module ietf-yang-schema-mount (prefix yangmnt) holds read-only state data under /schema-mounts. It has two lists. The namespace list maps prefixes to namespace URIs, for use in the XPath expressions of parent-reference. The mount-point list is keyed by module and label, and each entry specifies the schema for one mount point.

Each entry has an optional boolean config leaf (default true) and a mandatory choice called schema-ref with two cases, inline and shared-schema. Every mount point MUST be defined in a module that the server's YANG library lists with conformance type implement.

If several mount points with the same name exist in one module, for example because a grouping containing one is used more than once, the single list entry applies to all of them.
sections.eli5: The server keeps a read-only sign-up sheet that says, for each socket, which smaller model is plugged in and how it was described.

sections.title: Inline and Shared-Schema Mounting
sections.content:
The mounted schema is determined at run time. Every instance of the mount point that exists in the operational state MUST contain a copy of YANG library data that defines the mounted schema in exactly the same way as a top-level schema. A client is expected to retrieve this data from the instance tree.

The two ways differ in how much instances may vary. With inline, instances of the same mount point MAY use different mounted schemas. With shared-schema, all instances MUST use the same mounted schema, so they MUST have the same YANG library content identifier. In the inline case, equal content identifiers do not guarantee equal YANG library contents.

The config property of mounted nodes is overridden, making every node read-only (config false), if the mount point is itself config false or if the entry's config leaf is false.

Mounted modules MAY themselves contain mount points. A schema for such a nested mount point is specified by implementing ietf-yang-library and ietf-yang-schema-mount in the mounted schema, so there can be an arbitrary number of levels.
sections.eli5: Inline mounting is like letting each socket have its own different toy. Shared-schema is like making every socket take the same kind of toy.

sections.title: The Mount Jail and parent-reference
sections.content:
A fundamental principle is that a mounted schema works exactly like a top-level schema. All paths in it (in leafrefs, instance-identifiers, XPath expressions and augment targets) are interpreted with the mount point as the root. The RFC calls this the mount jail: mounted modules and their data cannot refer to anything outside it.

That is sometimes too strict. The RFC's example is network instances (RFC 8529), where each instance has its own routing engine but the list of interfaces is global. Routing configuration inside an instance needs to refer to interfaces in the parent schema.

For mount points using shared-schema, a leaf-list called parent-reference holds zero or more XPath 1.0 expressions. Each is evaluated with the node in the parent data tree where the mount point sits as the context node, and each MUST give a node-set. The union of these node-sets is added to the data tree that XPath expressions in the mounted schema can see.

Nodes made visible this way are available only for XPath evaluation. They cannot be accessed in the mounted schema through protocols such as NETCONF or RESTCONF.
sections.eli5: Normally a mounted model can only look at its own pieces, like a kid in a fenced yard. The parent-reference is a small window in the fence for looking at a few chosen things outside.

sections.title: RPCs, Notifications, NMDA and NACM
sections.content:
If a mounted module defines an RPC operation, clients can invoke it as if it were an action on the mount point. If the server emits a notification defined at the top level of a mounted module, it MUST be represented as if connected to the mount point. Because inline actions and notifications do not work inside a list without a key, mount points with such content SHOULD NOT have an ancestor list that lacks a key statement.

The mechanism works with servers that implement the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA, RFC 8342) and with older ones. A server without NMDA MAY implement revision 2016-06-21 of ietf-yang-library under a mount point. A server with NMDA MUST implement at least revision 2019-01-04.

If the Network Configuration Access Control Model (NACM, RFC 8341) is implemented, it controls access to mounted nodes in the same way as for top-level nodes. For the implementation, the RFC envisions shared management (one session sees parent and mounted data) and split management (a master session sees both, plus an extra session per mount point instance that sees only the mounted tree).
sections.eli5: A mounted model still follows the same rules about who may look or change things, and it can still send messages, as if it were part of the big model.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module's data is meant to be read through NETCONF or RESTCONF, whose mandatory-to-implement secure transports are SSH and TLS. NACM can restrict which users reach which content.

The one sensitive subtree called out is /schema-mounts. It describes the server's implementation, which may help an attacker find servers with known bugs, because vulnerabilities can be specific to particular modules, revisions, features or deviations. Read access to it should therefore be controlled, as should access to all nodes in mounted schemas.

Care is also needed when writing parent-reference expressions, because their results are added to the accessible tree for any XPath expression in the mounted schema.
sections.eli5: The list of what is plugged in where could help a bad guy pick a weak spot, so only the right people should be allowed to read it.
